introduction.p: Several function families occur frequently in calculus. Lines describe constant rates, polynomials and rational functions describe algebraic relationships, trigonometric functions describe periodic behavior, and exponentials describe constant proportional growth or decay. Logarithms invert exponentials. This section reviews their formulas, domains, and graphs.

subsection.p: Motion can repeat. A wheel turns. A pendulum swings. A tide rises and falls. A point on a spring oscillates.
The basic functions for periodic motion are sine and cosine.

subsection.p: The angle must be measured in radians for calculus.
A radian is not an arbitrary unit. It is defined by arc length:
On the unit circle, the radius is 1, so the radian measure of an angle equals the length of the arc it cuts off.

exercise.title: Why does calculus measure angles in radians?

statement.p: On the unit circle, cosine and sine are coordinates of a point reached by an angle. In your own words, what makes a radian a geometric unit rather than an arbitrary scale, and why will that choice matter for later derivative formulas?

hint.p: A radian is arc length divided by radius. On the unit circle, the angle equals the arc it cuts off. The clean limit \lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=1 uses that geometric scale.

subsection.title: Exponential functions
subsection.p: Linear functions add the same amount for each equal step. Exponential functions multiply by the same factor for each equal step.
If a>1, the function grows. If 0<a<1, the function decays.

exercise.title: How is exponential change different from linear change?

statement.p: Linear functions add the same amount for each equal step. Exponential functions multiply by the same factor. In your own words, what is the signature of f(x)=a^x, and why can exponential growth never output zero or a negative number?

hint.p: For a fixed step h, the identity a^{x+h}=a^x a^h multiplies the old output by the same factor no matter where the step begins. Powers of a positive base stay positive.

subsection.title: The catalog at a glance
subsection.p: This table is not a substitute for understanding the shapes. It is a map. When a problem mentions constant rate, think linear. When it mentions repeated percentage change, think exponential. When it mentions periodic motion, think trigonometric. When it mentions undoing an exponential, think logarithm.

A function family is a first guess, not a proof. The next step is modeling: choosing a function because units, data, and behavior suggest it. That will be our last preparation before limits turn “near” into a precise mathematical tool.
